Title: CUR-GAD: Calibrated Uncertainty and Risk Control for Graph Anomaly Detection
"CUR-GAD: Calibrated Uncertainty and Risk Control for Graph Anomaly Detection", Technical Disclosure. CUR-GAD: Calibrated Uncertainty and Risk Control for Graph Anomaly Detection. Graph Anomaly Detection (GAD) is critical in security-sensitive domains, yet faces reliability challenges: mis-calibrated confidence estimation (underconfidence in normal nodes, overconfidence in anomalies), adversarial vulnerability of derived confidence score under structural perturbations, and limited efficacy of conventional calibration methods for sparse anomaly patterns. Thus we propose CUR-GAD, a framework integrating statistical risk control into GAD via two innovations: (1) A Dual-Threshold Conformal Risk Control mechanism that provides theoretically guaranteed bounds for both False Negative Rate (FNR) and False Positive Rate (FPR) through providing prediction sets; (2) A Subgraph-aware Spectral Calibrator (SASC) that optimizes node representations through adaptive spectral filtering while reducing the size of prediction sets via hybrid loss optimization. Index Terms: Graph Anomaly Detection, Conformal Risk Control, Uncertainty Quantification, Calibration, Spectral Graph Neural Network. Graph-based anomaly detection (GAD) has become pivotal in security-critical applications like fraud detection [1] and misinformation identification [2], leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) through two paradigms: spatial methods enhance graph homophily through neighborhood redefinition or mitigate over-smoothing via adaptive message passing mechanisms [3]-[5], while spectral approaches design specialized filters to capture mid- and high-frequency signals induced by anomalous patterns [6], [7]. We therefore propose the CUR-GAD framework that generates prediction sets with theoretically guaranteed risk control - the expected FNR and FPR are provably bounded below pre-defined thresholds (e.g., 0.1). The conformal risk control framework operates by applying a post-hoc calibration mechanism to refine model f's predictions through a set-valued mapping Cλ : X → 2 Y . Published by Technical Disclosure Commons, 2025 FNR and FPR Control: Our framework integrates dual-threshold conformal risk control for false positive rate (CRC-FPR) and false negative rate (CRC-FNR), with final predictions derived through their intersection to ensure joint error control. Our CUR-GAD framework achieves provable statistical guarantees on FNR and FPR while incorporating a subgraph-aware spectral graph neural calibrator (SASC) that optimizes prediction set sizes without compromising statistical validity. So, it is important to remember that instruments and equipment will not always stay calibrated. At some point, the level of calibration will go down and it will affect the final measurements and quality of the products. A lot of different variables determine how frequently your instruments should be calibrated or re-calibrated. So, here is another thing to know about calibration frequency best practices. ### Calibration Frequency – Annually or Biannually. Some instruments need to be re-calibrated once or twice every year. If any instrument was damaged in an accident or if it sustained any kind of injury, you must calibrate it immediately. ### Calibration Frequency – As Needed by Projects. When you carry out certain assignments, you have to use certified and calibrated test equipment. Moreover, when assignments call for such calibration based on project requirements, you must follow it. Hence, this means that the instruments must be calibrated before the project starts. Also, you must calibrate all the instruments that were used after the project comes to an end. So, post-project calibration will show you if the testing that you conducted is indeed reliable or not. Some instruments, based on their use and functions, need to be calibrated frequently. Thus, if you deal with critical measurements quite frequently, it would be ideal that you conduct frequent and consistent calibration check-ups. ## Calibration Frequency Final Thoughts. # Calibration Techniques in Deep Neural Networks. Deep neural network classifiers have been shown to be mis-calibrated [1], i.e., their prediction probabilities are not reliable confidence estimates. For example, if a neural network classifies an image as a “dog” with probability *p*, *p* cannot be interpreted as the confidence of the network’s predicted class for the image. A calibrated neural network classifier outputs class probabilities that match the true correctness likelihood of the class in the ground truth dataset [1]. Calibrating neural networks is especially important in safety-critical applications where reliable confidence estimates are crucial for making informed decisions. These also include techniques that were not proposed as calibration techniques but have been shown to calibrate neural networks. Platt scaling [3] is a post-hoc calibration technique (i.e., applied after training a neural network) that uses the score (or logit) of the predicted class as an input feature to train a logistic regression model that outputs calibrated probabilities. Finally, the reliability diagrams below depict an uncalibrated Resnet-110 network compared with a Resnet-110 network calibrated with temperature scaling. [5] show that applying label smoothing results in implicit calibration of Neural Networks. The table also indicates that the effect of label smoothing and temperature scaling on neural network calibration are similar. In the paper “On mixup training: Improved calibration and predictive uncertainty for deep neural networks”, Thulasidasan et al. The plots below show that mixup has the **lowest ECE (calibration error)** with **a high test accuracy** compared with other calibration techniques like label smoothing across four datasets on the image classification task.
